intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Under each slide you will find how to read it, what to remember and where people slip. Each section page adds a worked example, so try it in pencil before you read the answer, then check yourself with the recall questions.

sections.title: What data feminism is
sections.big_idea: Data feminism asks **who made this data, about whom, for whom** before it asks what the data says, and it starts from the fact that power is unequal.
in_plain_words: Data feminism is a way of thinking about data and power, informed by intersectional feminism. It draws on a long line of thought: standpoint theory, Black feminist thought, intersectionality and participatory research. The book is a lens for judgement. It gives you prompts to apply to a real dataset and no checklist to tick.

The argument starts from a claim about the world: power is unequally distributed, and data both reflects that and can reshape it. Numbers carry the choices of the people who made them. South Asia's big systems, such as the Census, NFHS, Aadhaar and welfare rolls, raise the stakes because a small error rate touches millions. **Counting well is the goal**, and the course is pro-data.

key_terms.meaning: Thinking about data and power through intersectional feminism.
Compounded oppression across axes such as caste and gender (Crenshaw, 1989).
Reports one gap at a time, such as gender or caste, and misses the overlap.
Crossing two variables in one table to show where a burden compounds.
Knowledge is produced from a position, never from nowhere.

worked_example.title: Single-axis or intersectional?
worked_example.setup: A report offers four invented findings. Sort each as single-axis or intersectional.
steps: A: female literacy is lower than male literacy. One axis (gender), so single-axis.
B: literacy among Dalit women is lower than among other women and among Dalit men. Two axes crossed, so intersectional.
C: rural literacy trails urban literacy. One axis, so single-axis.
D: inside rural areas, women of the most excluded caste are furthest behind. Three axes crossed, so intersectional.
worked_example.answer: A and C are single-axis. B and D are intersectional, and only they show where the burden falls.

mistakes: Reading data feminism as a rulebook to apply mechanically. The deck calls it a lens, and mechanical use produces the box-ticking the book criticises.
Assuming it concerns women only. Feminism here is a lens on power and justice, and it applies well beyond gender.
Hearing the critique as anti-data. The course asks for more representative, accountable and honest counting.

recall.q: What is the core question of data feminism?
recall.a: Who made this data, about whom, for whom, and who benefits?

recall.q: Who coined intersectionality, and in which year?
recall.a: Kimberle Crenshaw, in 1989.

recall.q: Why does the course call the feminist critique pro-data?
recall.a: It asks for better data, and counting a harm is often the precondition for contesting it.

recall.q: Why does scale matter in South Asian data systems?
recall.a: An exclusion rate of one per cent in a national system is millions of people, and a category error is reproduced in every later dataset.

sections.title: Examine power
sections.big_idea: You cannot challenge what you have not named, so **find the mechanism**, usually a default or a form, and ask who it was built around.
in_plain_words: Examining power means reading the data setting along with the numbers: who funded the work, who designed the categories, who asked the questions, who was counted and who is absent. The enumerator row is easy to skip, yet their gender, caste and language shape answers on violence, income and decision-making.

Most exclusions come from reasonable people following standard practice. The privilege hazard explains why: a narrow design team cannot see failures its own lives never produce. The remedy is procedural. **Test the instrument with people unlike the designers**, and audit your defaults, such as one surname field or a head of household assumed to be male.

diagram.caption: the data setting, read in order

key_terms.meaning: The people, institutions, incentives and histories that produced a dataset.
Blind spots of a narrow, privileged design team that cannot see what excludes others.
A 'standard' form or category that quietly decides who fits.
A survey convention that often records the oldest man and lets him stand for the family.
Structural privilege that decides who collects data, about whom, and what numbers mean.

worked_example.title: Audit a form for defaults
worked_example.setup: An invented intake form has five fields. Use the table on slide 19 to find what each default excludes.
steps: One name field with one surname excludes mononyms and varied naming systems.
A single mobile number excludes shared household phones.
An address with a house number excludes informal settlements.
Male or female only excludes trans and non-binary respondents.
Self-completion by reading excludes non-readers.
worked_example.answer: Each default excludes a group nobody chose to exclude. Widen the fields and add a spoken option.

mistakes: Looking for a villain. Ask how the arrangement works, because a named mechanism invites a change to the form.
Letting a household head's answers stand for the household, which makes the women in it invisible.
Checking the instrument only with colleagues who resemble the designers.
Leaving the data-setting paragraph unwritten. It takes a paragraph and is routinely omitted.

recall.q: What is the privilege hazard?
recall.a: The danger that designers from a narrow privileged group cannot see the exclusions their position hides from them.

recall.q: Give the four steps of the data-setting chain.
recall.a: Who funded it, who designed the categories, who collected it, and who is counted or absent.

recall.q: Which row of the data-setting table is under-appreciated, and why?
recall.a: Who asked the questions. The enumerator's gender, caste and language change the answers.

recall.q: What is the remedy for the privilege hazard?
recall.a: Test the instrument with people unlike the designers before fielding, and treat every confusion as a design fault.

sections.title: Challenge power
sections.big_idea: Diagnosis is not enough: **count what is uncounted, audit the system, reframe the problem** and return data to the people it describes.
in_plain_words: Challenging power turns diagnosis into action. Counterdata is the sharpest tool. When a harm has no official category, or the body that would record it is the body accused, communities build the count themselves. The slides give registers of sanitation-worker deaths and people's audits of wage payments. Its strength is that it exists in a space that was blank.

Systems need auditing too. Ask whether error differs by group, what the model was trained on, who can contest a decision and whether the target is the real outcome. Then ask where the evidence goes. Most efforts stall between sharing and demanding, so **identify the forum first**: court, grievance body, legislature or press.

diagram.caption: four ways to contest power with data

key_terms.meaning: Data made by communities or activists to document a harm official systems fail to record.
A person wrongly left out of a scheme, who never appears in the system's own data.
A stand-in measure, such as past help, that can encode past inequity.
False positives and false negatives reported separately for each group.
The body with the power and duty to act on evidence, such as a court or grievance body.

worked_example.title: Compare error by group
worked_example.setup: An invented targeting system is tested on 100 eligible women and 100 eligible men. It wrongly excludes 30 women and 10 men.
steps: Women: 30 ÷ 100 = 30% wrongly excluded.
Men: 10 ÷ 100 = 10% wrongly excluded.
All eligible people: 40 ÷ 200 = 20%, an average that hides the split.
Compare the groups: 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so women face three times the exclusion error.
The excluded people do not appear in the system's data, so an outside list of eligible people is needed to find them.
worked_example.answer: The overall 20% conceals that women are excluded three times as often as men.

mistakes: Stopping at documentation. A report that records an injustice is not yet a challenge to it.
Treating missing records as proof of no harm where the recording body is the one accused.
Judging an algorithm by one overall accuracy figure instead of error disaggregated by group.
Watching only inclusion error. Exclusion error gets far less attention and does the quieter damage.

recall.q: What is counterdata?
recall.a: Data produced by communities or activists to document a harm that official systems fail to record.

recall.q: Name two situations that call for counterdata.
recall.a: A harm has no official category, reporting routes are inaccessible, the counting body is implicated, or the affected are not believed.

recall.q: Why is absence of records not evidence of absence?
recall.a: When the institution that would record a harm is the one accused of it, it has an interest in a low number.

recall.q: Between which steps do most data-for-justice efforts stall?
recall.a: Between sharing the evidence and demanding accountability, because no forum has the power and the obligation to act.

sections.title: Social audits and reframing the deficit
sections.big_idea: In a social audit the **people in the data read the data**, in public. Reframing moves the problem from the marginalised to the system.
in_plain_words: India's MGNREGA social audits turn the scheme's own records back on it. Villagers hear muster rolls and payments read aloud, then testify whether the work and wages were real. The slide records that MGNREGA was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025, which raises the guarantee to 125 days. The design lesson holds for either scheme.

Four features make it work: records read aloud so nobody needs literacy, testimony in the open, a statutory basis and formally recorded findings. It only works when findings are acted on, and with weak follow-up it becomes ritual. The second idea is framing. **Same data, opposite politics**: 'low participation' blames women, while 'an economy that does not count their work' blames the system.

right.title: System framing
items: An economy that does not count work
Schools that are unsafe or unreachable
A service that does not fit their lives

key_terms.meaning: A public hearing where records are read out and villagers testify against them.
The scheme's work and wage record, read aloud in the hearing.
A legal footing, so the audit cannot simply be refused.
Locating the problem in the marginalised group.
Locating the problem in structures, forms and services.
A route to put right what the audit finds.

worked_example.title: Rewrite a deficit sentence
worked_example.setup: Take the invented sentence 'Women show low scheme uptake' and test the framing with the table on slide 30.
steps: Locate the problem: the sentence places it in the women who did not enrol.
Find the system version in the table: 'A scheme people cannot access'.
Rewrite: 'Many eligible women could not access the scheme.'
Check the data: it is identical, and only the location of the problem has moved.
Say in the report why you chose this framing, because neither is automatically correct.
worked_example.answer: The numbers stay the same. The intervention that follows changes from changing women to changing access.

mistakes: Running a social audit as ritual. Where follow-up is weak, participants notice.
Assuming one framing is always correct. The skill is to notice which one you chose and to say why.
Presenting audit findings with no route to redress.

recall.q: Why can people join a social audit without being literate?
recall.a: The records are read aloud in public.

recall.q: What turns a social audit into ritual?
recall.a: Weak follow-up on its findings.

recall.q: Give one deficit framing and its system version.
recall.a: 'Poor school attendance' becomes 'schools that are unsafe or unreachable'.

recall.q: What does the slide say happened to MGNREGA?
recall.a: It was repealed from 1 July 2026 and replaced by the Viksit Bharat G RAM G Act 2025, which raises the guarantee to 125 days.

sections.title: Rethink binaries and hierarchies
sections.big_idea: Every category decides who counts. **Collect the finer variable**, add 'other, please specify', and count absences against a stated expectation.
in_plain_words: Binaries such as male and female, formal and informal, employed and unemployed are convenient for administration and lossy for analysis. A missing box does not remove a person from reality. It removes them from the record, and the dataset still looks complete. The cheap repair is an 'other, please specify' field. Legal recognition also runs ahead of forms, as the 2014 NALSA judgment shows.

Classifications also rank. Productive above reproductive kept care work outside GDP. Sen's missing women show a constructive use of categories: count an absence by setting what is against what should be. In the formula, **expected minus observed is the gap**. Categories change through sustained demand, and a statistician revising a manual changed none of them.

diagram.note: the system cannot count what it never saw, so the benchmark must come from outside

key_terms.meaning: A two-box classification that includes some realities and erases others.
A ranking hidden in a classification, such as skilled above unskilled.
Sen's count of women absent from Asia's populations against a benchmark ratio.
Girls per 1,000 boys aged 0 to 6; the deck gives roughly 952 as normal.
A field that turns an invisible exclusion into a visible, analysable one.
The term in a ranked pair that is treated as the normal case.

worked_example.title: Count an absence, Sen style
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district has 10,000 boys and 9,200 girls aged 0 to 6. Use the deck's benchmark of 952 girls per 1,000 boys.
steps: Observed girls: 9,200.
Observed ratio: 9,200 ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = 920 girls per 1,000 boys.
The gap is the finding. The next step is to ask why they are missing.
worked_example.answer: About 320 girls are missing against the benchmark, a ratio of 920 against 952.

mistakes: Forcing a binary for comparability and discarding the finer variable. You can collapse a detailed category later and never expand a collapsed one.
Reading a blank gender field as missing at random.
Assuming legal recognition means data recognition. A right that a form cannot record is hard to exercise.
Treating Sen's estimate as settled arithmetic. It has been debated and revised, and the method is what survives.

recall.q: What are the four outcomes when the box does not exist?
recall.a: The person misreports, is refused service, is guessed by the enumerator, or is left blank and treated as missing at random.

recall.q: What did Sen's method need?
recall.a: A biological benchmark ratio, the observed ratio, and the aggregated difference.

recall.q: Why is the employed and unemployed binary so consequential?
recall.a: The unemployment rate's denominator excludes anyone who has stopped looking.

recall.q: How does the Census treat a third gender?
recall.a: It has counted 'Others' since 2011, though the undercount is widely acknowledged.

recall.q: Which ranked pair kept unpaid care work out of GDP?
recall.a: Productive over reproductive work.

sections.title: Emotion and embodiment
sections.big_idea: Detachment is a stance. **Use feeling responsibly**: keep the person behind the row, ask consent, and respect knowledge held in bodies.
in_plain_words: The third principle questions the myth of the cold analyst, a position usually open to people the data does not hurt. It does not claim that feeling improves accuracy. A bare chart is a persuasive choice too. In development data a row is a woman who walked for water or a girl whose family made a decision, and remembering that changes how carefully you store and share the file.

Visceralisation makes numbers felt, for example a classroom of children in place of a total. Each technique moves risk to the people depicted, so use the ethical test: would the subject recognise this, whose reaction is centred, who chose the framing. Embodied knowledge, such as an ASHA's sense of which hamlet is hungry, is **real data that arrives early**.

key_terms.meaning: Representing data so it is felt through the body and emotions as well as seen.
Knowledge held in bodies and lived experience as well as in spreadsheets.
Exploiting suffering for shock value and stripping dignity.
The idea that good data work must be cold and neutral.
The real person a data row stands for.

worked_example.title: Apply the four ethical questions
worked_example.setup: An invented fundraising poster shows a named woman beside a total. Apply the four questions on slide 46.
steps: Would the subject recognise this? Ask whether you have shown it to her.
Does it restore context, or strip it for effect?
Whose reaction is centred, hers or the donor's?
Who chose the framing, she or you?
If you cannot ask her, treat that as a reason for restraint.
worked_example.answer: Hold the poster until she has seen it and shaped the framing. Without that, change the design.

mistakes: Using emotion for shock, which moves the donor's reaction to the centre.
Dismissing frontline knowledge as merely anecdotal. The slide calls that a power move.
Naming people in a story without their consent.
Treating a plain chart as free of rhetoric. Austerity is a rhetorical choice too.

recall.q: What is data visceralisation?
recall.a: Representations of data experienced through the body and emotions, seen and also felt.

recall.q: Name two of the four ethical questions for emotional imagery.
recall.a: Would the subject recognise it, does it restore context, whose reaction is centred, who chose the framing.

recall.q: Why is frontline knowledge often earlier than statistics?
recall.a: It is available months before the corresponding statistic, and it is discarded because it has no format.

recall.q: How can a system act on frontline knowledge?
recall.a: A structured question in a monthly meeting, recorded, without pretending it is a measurement.

sections.title: Consider context
sections.big_idea: A number outside its context can reverse its meaning. **Write the denominator, the method and the gap into the sentence.**
in_plain_words: The sixth principle says numbers do not speak for themselves. Raw data is an oxymoron: before you see a dataset it has been defined, collected, coded, cleaned and selected. Ninety per cent institutional delivery sounds like success until you ask what institutional means, who the missing ten per cent are and where referrals are counted.

Provenance matters because administrative statistics measure the meeting of a population and an institution. A higher count may mean a worse problem or a better reporting system. Aggregation also strips context, from village to district and from household to person. Some comparisons should be refused, with the reason stated. **Write context into the sentence**, since a footnote does not travel.

diagram.note: each addition is one clause in the sentence

key_terms.meaning: A contradiction: data is always defined, collected, coded, cleaned and selected.
Where data comes from and which system produced it.
A stand-in measure, such as delivery location for safety.
Who is in the base of a rate.
Combining units upward, which dissolves the outlier, the district or the woman inside the household.

worked_example.title: Add context to 90%
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district records 400 births in a quarter, 360 of them in facilities.
steps: Institutional share: 360 ÷ 400 = 90%.
Births outside facilities: 400 − 360 = 40.
Suppose 30 of those 40 were in the remotest hamlets: 30 ÷ 40 = 75%.
Define institutional, say where referrals are counted, and add an outcome measure beside delivery location.
worked_example.answer: The 90% is correct as stated, and the sentence still needs the definition, who the other 10% are, and an outcome.

mistakes: Ranking areas by recorded crime or reported violence. That measures policing and reporting as much as the harm.
Parking caveats in a methods annex. The number will be quoted, and the annex will not.
Reading household data as if it described the woman inside the household.
Refusing a comparison without saying why in the report.

recall.q: What does 'raw data is an oxymoron' mean?
recall.a: By the time anyone analyses it, data has already been defined, collected, coded, cleaned and selected.

recall.q: Why can a state with better reporting look worse?
recall.a: Better reporting infrastructure records more cases, so a naive ranking punishes it.

recall.q: Which aggregation step is most specific to gender analysis?
recall.a: Household to person, because household data cannot see intra-household allocation.

recall.q: Name the four contextualising steps.
recall.a: State the denominator, say how it was collected, flag the known gap and give the historical condition.

sections.title: Make labour visible
sections.big_idea: Every dataset rests on **uncredited labour**: respondents, field staff, clerks and annotators. Credit is free, fair pay costs money, and both improve data.
in_plain_words: The seventh principle credits the work behind the data. The credit gradient runs opposite to the effort gradient: the analyst gets the byline, while respondents, field workers and clerks get little or none. It maps onto gender, class and caste. Underpaid, rushed fieldwork produces the measurement error that later looks like a statistical problem.

Frontline data work is often care work. An ASHA, an anganwadi worker or an enumerator persuades, counsels and builds trust, yet only the data half appears in the costing. Unpaid care is the largest invisible labour, which is why the 2019 Time Use Survey counts as a data-feminist act. Respondents give hours too, so **return findings as a budgeted deliverable**.

key_terms.meaning: Credit falls as you move from the analyst down to the respondent.
A payment that is not a salary, used for several frontline roles.
The time and emotional cost borne by people who answer surveys.
The rational response of over-studied communities that get nothing back.
Labelling training data, often piece-rate work in the Global South.

worked_example.title: Who is usually credited?
worked_example.setup: Use the table on slide 58 to place each kind of labour in a dataset.
steps: Respondent time: usually not credited.
Enumerator fieldwork: rarely credited.
Data entry and cleaning: almost never credited.
Supervision and quality control: rarely credited.
Analysis and writing: credited, through the byline.
worked_example.answer: Credit rises toward the analyst. Name the field team in the acknowledgements and budget realistic pay for the bottom three stages.

mistakes: Calling sustained, required work 'volunteer'. That is a wage decision described as a category.
Reading survey fatigue as laziness.
Skipping the pay question when buying annotation or moderation from a vendor.
Treating a credit line as enough. Paying properly is the substantive version.

recall.q: Which stage of the pipeline usually gets the byline?
recall.a: The analysts.

recall.q: Why is realistic budgeting for fieldwork a data-quality step?
recall.a: Underpaid, rushed fieldwork produces the measurement error that later appears as a statistical problem.

recall.q: What does the 2019 Time Use Survey make visible?
recall.a: The hours of unpaid care work that national accounts had long ignored.

recall.q: What is the minimum reciprocity owed to respondents?
recall.a: Returning findings to the community, budgeted as a deliverable.

sections.title: Embrace pluralism
sections.big_idea: Pluralism changes **who decides** what gets measured. If the answers could not have changed the design, the process produced legitimacy and little knowledge.
in_plain_words: The fifth principle asks for many voices and forms of knowledge. The people closest to the problem are closest to the solution, and often to the missing data. Compare extractive and participatory practice by who defines the question, who collects, who holds the data and who benefits first. Leaving a usable copy with the community costs almost nothing.

Token consultation gathers views after decisions, with no follow-up and no power over the budget. Real pluralism shares decision rights, or says plainly that it cannot. Haraway's point that all knowledge is situated supports a positionality note. At its deepest, **communities co-design the indicator**, which gains validity and costs comparability, so report a common core and local indicators side by side.

children.label: Which knowledge counts
items: People who did not use the service

children.label: How it is recorded
items: Oral history, maps, story and art

key_terms.meaning: Outsiders arrive, survey and leave, and the value flows outward.
The community defines, collects, interprets and keeps the data.
Haraway's idea that all knowledge is seen from somewhere, by someone.
A short paragraph on who did the work and how that shaped it.
Letting communities help decide the questions as well as answer them.
Gathering views you have already decided to ignore.

worked_example.title: Is this consultation real?
worked_example.setup: An invented project holds one workshop after the budget is fixed. Test it with slide 66's question and the table on slide 70.
steps: Ask whether the answers could have changed the design. The budget is fixed, so they could not.
Row 1 of the table: views gathered after decisions mark token consultation.
Row 2: a workshop with no follow-up is also token.
Fix one: gather views before the budget is set.
Fix two: return findings with what changed, and transfer some decision rights. If power cannot be shared, say so.
worked_example.answer: As planned it is token consultation. Moving the workshop earlier and reporting back makes it a real input.

mistakes: Adding a consultation annex and calling it pluralism.
Inviting the same few articulate participants every time.
Assuming participatory collection is automatically more accurate. It can improve or worsen quality.
Reading Haraway as relativism. She argues that naming your position makes objectivity more achievable.

recall.q: Which question tests a participatory process?
recall.a: Could the answers have changed the design?

recall.q: Why sample non-users of a service?
recall.a: They can explain the exclusion, and the finding often changes the design.

recall.q: What trade-off do co-designed indicators carry?
recall.a: They are more valid and legitimate but harder to compare across sites.

recall.q: What is the practical form of situated knowledge?
recall.a: A positionality note, normal in qualitative research and rare in quantitative.

sections.title: The matrix of domination
sections.big_idea: Power interlocks across four areas, so **diagnose where an injustice lives** and cross at least two axes to see who is at the bottom.
in_plain_words: Collins' matrix says systems of power interlock and operate in four areas: structural, disciplinary, hegemonic and interpersonal. Matching the intervention to the area matters. Most data-quality effort goes to the fourth, through enumerator training, because it is nearest to hand, yet most injustices start in the first two. Training cannot fix an exclusion built into the sampling frame.

Crenshaw's legal cases have a data analogue: a report with a gender chapter and a caste chapter and no table crossing them. Everyone sits on the matrix, advantaged on one axis and disadvantaged on another. You cannot disaggregate by everything, so **name the intersection your work most affects** and plan the sample at the design stage, often by oversampling.

key_terms.meaning: Collins' framework for how systems of power interlock across four areas.
Laws and institutions that organise oppression.
Bureaucratic rules that enforce it unevenly.
Culture and ideas that make it seem natural.
Everyday lived experience of it.
Sampling the group of interest more heavily so it can be seen.

worked_example.title: Place each injustice in its area
worked_example.setup: Four problems from the table on slide 75 arrive in one audit.
steps: The census is designed to count a narrow set of people: structural. Target law and mandate.
One group's claims are verified while another's are waved through: disciplinary. Target rules and procedures.
'Head of household' is assumed to be male: hegemonic. Target framing and narrative.
An enumerator skips the women's answers: interpersonal. Target training and supervision.
worked_example.answer: Structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, interpersonal, each with its own remedy target.

mistakes: Trying to fix a structural exclusion with enumerator training.
Disaggregating by gender or caste but never both.
Using the matrix to sort people into oppressed and oppressor camps. It describes positions.
Planning the crossing at analysis. The sample has to support it at design.

recall.q: Name the four areas of the matrix.
recall.a: Structural, disciplinary, hegemonic and interpersonal.

recall.q: Where does the framework come from?
recall.a: Patricia Hill Collins, Black Feminist Thought (1990).

recall.q: Why must the crossing be planned at sampling?
recall.a: A dataset that cannot support the crossing cannot be made to later.

recall.q: What should you say when a group is absent from your data?
recall.a: Say so, so the reader does not take the list of groups as complete.

sections.title: Gender data gaps in South Asia
sections.big_idea: What is not counted is not budgeted for. **Ask women directly, disaggregate by default, and read survey figures on violence as a floor.**
in_plain_words: The gender data gap is the privilege hazard at the scale of a whole statistical system. Gaps come in four types, and the last two, collected but not disaggregated and collected but not analysed, are cheapest to fix. Check existing datasets before commissioning new collection. Criado Perez's default male shows the cost: a world built on average-man data calls the misfit normal.

India's Time Use Survey 2019 made unpaid care an official number, and NFHS-5 asks women directly about decisions, violence, accounts and phones. Even so, survey figures on violence are a floor, so write 'at least X per cent'. As services go digital, **who holds the phone shapes who appears in the data**. Being counted helps only if the counting serves the counted.

key_terms.meaning: Systematic absence of sex-disaggregated and gender-relevant data.
Criado Perez's term for treating the average man as the standard case.
Too few free hours, because of unpaid work.
A survey figure read as 'at least this many'.
Women's lower phone ownership and mobile internet use, which skews digital data.

worked_example.title: Write the floor sentence
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survey finds 30 of every 100 married women report spousal violence.
steps: Share reporting: 30 ÷ 100 = 30%.
Check the barriers: shame, fear, normalisation and lack of privacy all push the figure down.
No plausible mechanism pushes it up, so the figure is a floor.
Wrong: '30 per cent of women experience violence.' Right: 'At least 30 per cent of women reported violence.'
worked_example.answer: Report 'at least 30 per cent', and read the gap to reality as evidence of the power that enforces silence.

mistakes: Reading a survey number on violence as a ceiling.
Using the household head to report on women's status.
Running a digital-only survey or grievance route and calling the sample complete.
Equating being counted with being helped.

recall.q: What are the four types of gender data gap?
recall.a: Not collected at all, collected but not disaggregated, collected via a proxy, and collected but not analysed.

recall.q: Why does NFHS-5 ask women directly?
recall.a: A proxy would report the household norm, and the household phone is not her phone.

recall.q: Which two gap types are cheapest to fix?
recall.a: Collected but not disaggregated, and collected but not analysed.

recall.q: Name two barriers to disclosing violence.
recall.a: Shame and blame, fear of consequences, normalisation, or lack of privacy in the interview.

sections.title: Practice and tools
sections.big_idea: Pick two principles and make them habits. **Refuse the average, protect small cells, and run the checklist on your last output.**
in_plain_words: The seven principles come down to seven questions and seven five-minute actions, such as writing the data-setting paragraph, adding an 'other, specify' field, sampling non-users and naming the field team. None needs a new method or budget. Pick two and make them habits, since one principle applied consistently beats seven applied once for a workshop.

Disaggregation is the everyday tool: sex first, then caste, disability, region and wealth. It carries a risk, because small cells can re-identify people and categories can stigmatise. Report cell sizes and uncertainty, and suppress cells below about 25 unweighted cases. Avoid the five pitfalls on the slides, above all **assuming that more data means more justice**.

diagram.caption: the practice loop in five steps

key_terms.meaning: Breaking a headline number down by sex, caste, disability, region and wealth.
A group with so few cases that individuals may be identified or the estimate is imprecise.
Withholding figures for cells below a threshold of about 25 unweighted cases.
Six questions to run on a finished output to find unasked questions.

worked_example.title: Apply the small-cell rule
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a crossed table has four cells with 18, 140, 22 and 160 unweighted cases. Use the threshold on slide 96.
steps: The threshold is about 25 unweighted cases.
18 and 22 fall under 25, so flag or suppress those two cells.
Report the other two with uncertainty and state that the smallest groups cannot be shown.
worked_example.answer: Two of the four cells are flagged. Say in the report that the crossing is limited by sample size.

mistakes: Reporting an average and calling the analysis done.
Disaggregating by one axis and ignoring the intersection.
Publishing small cells with no suppression or flag.
Counting people without ever returning value to them.

recall.q: Which operational habit is the core of the course?
recall.a: Disaggregation: never settle for the average.

recall.q: Give two protections when you disaggregate.
recall.a: Suppress or flag small cells, report uncertainty, check consent covers the use, or ask whether naming helps or harms.

recall.q: Why run the checklist on your last output?
recall.a: It is easier to see, and it tells you which habit to change.

recall.q: Why is 'more data' not the answer by itself?
recall.a: More data collected the same way reproduces the same exclusions at greater cost.

notes.2: The agenda lists eleven topics. The principles do not come in numbered order, so use the principle label on each section's first slide to find it. Skim the list now and note which topic matches your daily work, since that is where to read first.
notes.4: Use the table to avoid two easy errors. The book gives you a lens for questions and offers no methods manual to copy. Begin every dataset with the core question, **who made this, about whom, for whom**, before you ask what the numbers say.
notes.5: Pick a dataset you use and list the five choices in the table: what was measured, which categories, whom asked, what left out, how shown. You will find all five. The remedy is plain: **write the decisions down** so a reader can see where values entered.
notes.6: Notice the order of the definition. It starts with a claim about power in the world, and the claim about data follows from it. That is why better statistics cannot settle the argument. The lens is **intersectional**, so look at more than one axis at once.
notes.7: Hold on to the practical point at the bottom: **cross-tabulate instead of controlling**. Controlling for caste removes it from view. Crossing by caste and gender shows where the burden falls, for example on Dalit women specifically.
notes.8: Ask the three questions at the top: who collects, about whom, for whom. Then test your own sector against the table. **People with fewer institutional contacts leave fewer traces**, so the groups you know least about are often the larger ones.
notes.9: Learn the seven as questions you put to your own work. If seven is too many, the slide gives you a start: keep **examine power** and **consider context**. They are not a sequence, and any one applied seriously to a real dataset will produce useful work.
notes.10: Do not read this course as hostile to numbers. The right-hand column lists what the critique does not ask for. Counting can be an act of care, since counting a harm is often the first step to contesting it. The tension is that **being counted can also mean being watched**.
notes.11: This slide answers the charge that data feminism is a fashion. Five traditions sit under it, none built for data science, and standpoint theory has been argued over since the 1970s. Remember the shared idea: **knowledge is produced from a position**.
notes.12: Scale is the argument here. Census, NFHS, Aadhaar and welfare rolls each touch a very large population, so a small error rate means **millions of people** wrongly counted. A category error in a national system also flows into every later dataset built on it.
notes.14: Examining power comes first because you cannot challenge what you have not named. Aim at the mechanism and skip the blame. A named mechanism invites a change to the form, while a named villain only invites a defence. Ask **who is advantaged by the default**.
notes.15: Treat the dataset as the visible tip. Walk down the four steps: who paid, who designed the categories, who collected under what pressure, who is counted or absent. Do not skip the enumerator row. Their gender, caste and language shape answers on **violence, income and decision-making**.
notes.16: Use the two lists as a ritual before you analyse, because answers found afterwards become caveats. The first list questions the data and the second questions its use. If you can answer only one, choose **who benefits from the framing**: it changes conclusions most often.
notes.17: The hazard is about blind spots and leaves character out of it. A team drawn from one narrow group cannot see failures its own lives never produce. The fix is procedural: **test the instrument with people unlike the designers** and count every confusion as a design fault.
notes.18: Read the shape of the chart and ignore the exact values, because the slide labels them illustrative. The pattern is that women thin out toward the people who decide what gets measured. This links to the previous slide: the hazard is **structural**, a feature of who is in the room.
notes.19: Defaults work because nobody has to decide anything. Match each default in the table to the group it leaves out, from mononyms to non-readers. Then try the exercise: **audit your own forms once**. It takes two hours and typically finds three or four exclusions.
notes.20: Follow the chain in the table. If the head's caste, education and answers stand for everyone, inter-group households, women's education and women's work vanish. Where your data allows it, **prefer a designated respondent** or interview women directly, and say why in the report.
notes.21: Do not hunt for a villain. Power here runs through ordinary things: a form, a default field, a best-practice indicator. Practise **making the ordinary strange** by asking who each choice serves and who it costs. Fixes are often small, such as one added field.
notes.23: Diagnosis and action are separate skills. Use the table to check whether your project does any of the four things. A report that documents an injustice has not yet challenged it. At the design stage, ask **who will act on this and what they can actually do**.
notes.24: Counterdata fills a blank. The table tells you when it is warranted: no category exists, reporting routes are blocked, the counting body has a stake, or the affected are not believed. Remember the sharpest case: where the accused institution does the recording, **silence is not evidence of absence**.
notes.25: Look at what the four examples share. Each sets many small reports or testimonies against an official figure, and that comparison forces a reconciliation. Expect pushback on method, so **document your collection protocol** well enough that the work cannot be waved away.
notes.26: An algorithm trained on past decisions repeats them. Run the four audit questions on any scoring or targeting system you meet. The deepest is the last: whether the target is the real outcome or a proxy. **Wrongly excluded people never appear in the system's own data.**
notes.27: Read this as a reminder that a record is a fraction of reality. The values are illustrative, so use the shape: the reported count sits far below the estimated actual. **Reading only reported cases mistakes the visible fraction for the whole** and treats silence as safety.
notes.28: Learn the four steps as a ladder: document, share, demand, change. The table gives the usual snag at each rung. Most efforts stall between sharing and demanding, because **no forum has both the power and the duty to act**. Find that forum first.
notes.30: Same data, opposite politics. Use the table to rewrite your own sentences, moving each deficit phrase on the left to its system phrase on the right. Neither framing is automatically correct. The discipline is to **notice your choice and say why**.
notes.32: Binaries are convenient for administration and lossy for analysis. Skim the table for the finer reality each one hides, such as the blurred middle in formal and informal work. Keep one rule: **collect the finer variable**, because you can collapse a detailed category later and never expand a collapsed one.
notes.33: Look at the four outcomes of a missing box. All four leave a dataset that looks complete, which is why a missing category is dangerous. The cheap repair is an **'other, please specify'** field, which converts an invisible exclusion into one you can analyse.
notes.34: Law and data move at different speeds. The table shows recognition running ahead of record-keeping, and a right that a form cannot record is hard to use. Your own action is small: **add the category to your instruments** and record the count accurately even when it is tiny.
notes.35: Sen counted people who are absent. Remember his three steps: set a benchmark ratio, observe the real ratio, aggregate the difference. The estimate is debated, as the slide says. **The method survives the arithmetic dispute**: compare what is with a stated expectation of what should be.
notes.36: The chart shows the pattern in the youngest cohort. The slide gives roughly 952 girls per 1,000 boys as the biologically normal benchmark, and any shortfall is Sen's missing women made visible. Read it as **a hierarchy of value written in the count**.
notes.37: Use the table to see who falls between each pair of boxes. Employed and unemployed is the most consequential pair, because the unemployment rate's denominator drops anyone who has stopped looking. When a standard forces a binary, **report the standard measure and the finer one** together.
notes.38: A classification can rank as well as sort. Read your own category list and ask which term is the unmarked default. Remember the pair with the biggest measured consequence: **productive versus reproductive**, which kept unpaid care work outside GDP and most statistics for a century.
notes.39: To count an absence you need a benchmark from outside the system, because the system cannot record what it never saw. Follow the four steps: model who should be present, count who is, treat the gap as the finding, ask why. **Two independent sources** are the general method.
notes.40: Categories change when people demand it. Each row in the table was driven by litigation, advocacy or politics, and a statistician revising a manual changed none of them. If you want a system improved, expect the route to run through **sustained demand and legal pressure**.
notes.42: The detached analyst is a position, usually open to people the data does not hurt. The slide does not say that feeling improves accuracy. It says **the appearance of detachment is a design choice** that persuades. A bare bar chart also makes a claim: that the number speaks for itself.
notes.43: Keep the referent in mind: each row is a person. The table translates four rows into lives. This changes decisions, such as whether a small cell deserves investigation and whether rounding hides someone. It also changes how you **store and share** a file of people.
notes.44: Visceralisation means data you feel in the body as well as see. Each technique in the table makes an abstraction concrete and passes risk to the people depicted. Use the closing test: **would the person depicted recognise and accept the representation?** If you cannot ask, be cautious.
notes.45: Separate responsible from irresponsible use of emotion with the table. The line runs between restoring context and agency and removing them for effect. A quick check from the slide: **would the piece still work if its subject read it?** That question settles most cases.
notes.46: Ask these four questions in a design meeting; they take two minutes. Would the subject recognise this, does it restore context, whose reaction is centred, who chose the framing. If you cannot ask the subject, treat that as **a reason for restraint** and give it real weight.
notes.47: Treat frontline knowledge as data that arrives early. The ASHA, teacher and midwife in the table know before any statistic is compiled, and the system discards it because it has no format. The fix is modest: **a structured question in a monthly meeting, recorded**.
notes.48: These are ordinary communication choices, made deliberately or by default. Pick one: choose units a reader can feel, pair a chart with testimony, or name places with consent. Unit choice carries most of the effect: **'one in three' and 'thirty-three per cent'** read differently.
notes.50: A number outside its context can mislead more than inform. Test each quoted figure in the table by asking what is missing, such as the definition of literate. The missing context can reverse the meaning, so **write it into the sentence**. Numbers travel and footnotes do not.
notes.51: Follow the four steps to see why 'raw data' is a contradiction: a measurement is chosen, a category imposed, values cleaned and recoded. The table names the people behind each stage. The response is documentation, since **a dataset whose cooking is written down** earns more trust.
notes.52: Work this example slowly. Ninety per cent institutional delivery sounds like success until you ask what institutional means, who the missing ten per cent are and where referrals are counted. Remember the lesson on proxies: **delivery location stands in for safety**, so add an outcome measure beside it.
notes.53: Refusing a comparison is an analytical decision with reasons, so give the reasons in the report. Rankings of recorded crime or reported violence measure policing and reporting as much as the harm itself. A **state with better reporting records more cases**, and a naive ranking punishes it.
notes.54: Turn context into clauses. The table gives one sentence for each step: denominator, collection method, known gap, historical condition. Put them in the sentence itself. The number will be quoted and a methods annex will not, so **a clause travels where an annex stays behind**.
notes.55: Provenance means tracing what a statistic measures. Each row pairs a number with the system behind it. A higher count can mean a worse problem or a **better reporting system**. Without provenance you cannot tell which, and testing or diagnosis rates are the clearest case.
notes.56: Every step up the ladder erases someone: village, district, state, household, person. The gender-specific one is household to person, because household data cannot see allocation inside the home. As a default, **report the disaggregation beside the aggregate**. The aggregate travels, and the disaggregation is what is true.
notes.58: The seventh principle credits the work behind the data. The table shows credit running opposite to effort, with the byline reserved for analysis. A cheap first step is naming the field team in the acknowledgements. The **substantive step is paying them properly**.
notes.59: Read the chain from respondents to analysts and notice who is paid, credited and published at each stage. Rushed, underpaid fieldwork creates the measurement error that later looks like a statistical problem. So **budgeting realistically for the bottom three rows** improves data quality as well as fairness.
notes.60: The same person does the data work and the care work, yet only one half appears in a job description or costing. The slide gives three roles: ASHA, anganwadi worker, enumerator. The status of honorarium roles is **a live policy question** that litigation and unions have contested.
notes.61: Time-use surveys changed what counts. The table traces how leaving unpaid care out of GDP and labour statistics makes women appear 'not working' and lets designs assume free time. Measuring hours is uncontroversial and gives a designer most of what is needed. **Valuing them in money is still debated.**
notes.62: Four steps from visibility to fairness. Crediting collectors and entry staff costs a line in the acknowledgements and is the one most often skipped, so the barrier is habit. Check your budgets for the word 'volunteer': **applied to required, sustained work, it is a wage decision**.
notes.63: Count the respondent's hour as a cost. The table shows who pays most: women asked about the household, survivors of sensitive questions, over-studied communities. Survey fatigue is a rational response to giving data and getting nothing back. Make **returning findings a budgeted deliverable**.
notes.64: The chain of hidden hands reaches from the village enumerator to the annotators who label AI training data. Use the table to spot invisible work in your own projects. If you buy any of these services, **ask the vendor what the workers are paid**. It is rarely asked.
notes.66: The table separates real pluralism from lookalikes by authority. Consultation annexes, validation and averaging opinions all leave decision power where it was. Use the closing test: **could the answers have changed the design?** If they could not, the process produces legitimacy and little knowledge.
notes.67: Local knowledge is data too. Read the table for who knows what. The slide stresses people who did not take up a service, since they can explain the exclusion, and that group is the least often collected. **Sample non-users** to find the finding that changes the design.
notes.68: Compare the two columns row by row: who defines the question, who collects, who holds the data, who benefits first. The easiest to change is the third, because **leaving a usable copy with the community costs almost nothing**. Participation is not automatically more accurate, so justify it on its own terms.
notes.69: Evidence depends on protocol. In each row the condition on the right is a stated way the material was produced, such as recorded with consent or georeferenced. Aim to **design qualitative and quantitative work together**. Appending interview quotes to a finished statistical report does not meet that standard.
notes.70: Consultation after the decision extracts time and changes nothing, which can be worse than not asking because it spends goodwill the next process needs. Use the table to check your own process. If power cannot be shared, **say so plainly**: 'we are gathering views to inform a decision we will make'.
notes.71: Haraway's point is often read as relativism, and the slide says it is the opposite. Naming your standpoint makes objectivity more achievable. Put it into practice with **a positionality note**: a short paragraph on who did the work and how that shaped it. It is rare in quantitative work.
notes.72: Co-design is the deepest pluralism: the community helps decide the questions. The table shows how each decision (what safety means, the threshold, the comparison) shapes the indicator. The cost is comparability. The compromise is **a common core plus local indicators**, reported separately and labelled.
notes.74: Collins' matrix is the backbone of the course. Remember two ideas: systems interlock, and there are four places where power operates. Its use is diagnostic. Work out which place a data injustice lives in, because that tells you whether the remedy is **a law, a rule, a narrative or a practice**.
notes.75: Learn the four areas with one data example each: structural, disciplinary, hegemonic, interpersonal. The second table links each to a remedy target. Most data-quality effort goes to the fourth because it is nearest, yet **most injustices start in the first two**. Enumerator training cannot fix a sampling frame.
notes.76: Connect the legal history to your tables. Courts failed Black women because the categories assumed a typical woman or a typical Black person. The data version is a report with a gender chapter, a caste chapter and **no table crossing them**. Intersectional questions need intersectional tables.
notes.77: The chart is illustrative, so read its shape. Gender alone shows a gap, and both axes crossed show where the two compound. Only the crossed table reveals this. If your sample cannot support the crossing, **report that limitation** and avoid substituting two single-axis figures for it.
notes.78: Each row names what a single axis hides: which women, which members of a group, who inside rural. The bottom position in the crossed table is rarely additive, and that is what compounding means. Where the sample cannot support it, **say so**, because that is itself a data-gap finding.
notes.79: Turn the matrix into four steps: locate the area, cross two axes, name your intersection, design collection for it. The fourth must happen at sampling, since a dataset cannot support later a crossing it was not built for. **Oversampling the group of interest** is the standard technique.
notes.80: Everyone has a position on the matrix. The table shows people advantaged on one axis and disadvantaged on another, which guards against a single victim or villain story. Apply it inward too: your own position decides **which exclusions you are likely to notice**.
notes.81: The matrix has many axes, but sample sizes forbid disaggregating by all of them. So choose: **name the intersection your work most affects** and design to see it clearly. The lower rows of the table are often not asked at all, so state who is absent from your data.
notes.83: Gender data gaps come in four types. The last two, collected but not disaggregated and collected but not analysed, are cheapest to fix because the variable already sits in the file. Before commissioning new collection, **check what lies unanalysed** in existing datasets.
notes.84: Criado Perez shows the default male at work in products and trials. The slide stresses that no malice is involved: the default was inherited and never questioned. Take the exercise to your own sector and ask what the **standard case** is and who does not fit it.
notes.85: The chart values are illustrative, patterned on the 2019 survey. The lesson is that women do far more unpaid work and men far more paid work. For design, the issue is time: an activity asking two hours a week asks for hours she lacks. **One activity per slot undercounts care.**
notes.86: India's 2019 time-use survey made women's unpaid work an official number. Follow the table from what it makes visible to what that enables. For programme design, take **time poverty** as the most actionable finding, because it tells you what your activity is competing with.
notes.87: NFHS-5 asks women directly. The table shows why that matters: a proxy reports the household norm, violence cannot be asked in company, and a household phone is not her phone. This is also why **NFHS and administrative figures often disagree**, since administrative data reflects the household or the facility.
notes.88: Treat every GBV statistic as a floor. All four barriers push the number down and nothing pushes it up. So write 'at least X per cent' in the sentence, since **'X per cent of women experience' is inaccurate**. The gap between reported and real is itself evidence of the power that enforces silence.
notes.89: Closing the gap is mostly cheap. Three of the five steps cost almost nothing, and the slide's claim is that the gap persists because **nobody is required to close it**. So the highest-impact action is writing these steps into the terms of reference for any data collection you commission.
notes.90: Digital collection quietly samples men more. Go down the table: the respondent owns a phone, controls it, can use mobile internet, and the number identifies one person. Each assumption fails more often for women, and the dataset still looks complete. Keep **a non-digital route** open.
notes.91: Being counted can open a benefit or enable policing. The tension does not resolve into a rule, so ask of each system whether **the counting serves the counted**. The table lines up the four outcomes and shows why consent and protection matter beside disaggregation.
notes.93: Use the first table as a question for each principle and the second as the five-minute version. None needs a new method or budget. The slide's advice: **pick two and make them habits** before adding the rest. One principle applied consistently beats seven applied once for a workshop.
notes.94: Run the six questions on your last output before your next one. The table lists failing answers that sound reasonable, and each is what a competent report says when the question was never asked. Build the habit of **asking the question**, whatever the reply sounds like.
notes.95: If you adopt one habit, make it this: never settle for the average. Break it down by sex, then caste, disability, region and wealth. The table says what each typically reveals. It is cheap, since **the variables are usually in the dataset already** and the cost is a few more rows.
notes.96: Visibility cuts both ways. Cross-tabulate, report cell sizes and uncertainty, and centre the most marginalised. Then check the four protections: flag small cells, report uncertainty, confirm consent, ask whether naming helps. The slide offers **suppressing cells below about 25 unweighted cases** as a convention.
notes.97: Five pitfalls with one root: forgetting that data is about people. Match each to its correction in the table. Hold on to the fourth: **more data collected the same way reproduces the same exclusions at greater cost**. Ask what the data will be used for.
notes.98: Use this as a study plan. Pair one theory source with one dataset, such as NFHS or the Time Use Survey. The principles are easier to hold once you have applied them to a file with real gaps. The Indian sources are free, so a sceptical reader can **check your claim**.
notes.99: Five takeaways, each reduced to one question in the table. Ask them of any dataset, dashboard and report. If you keep only one, keep the third: **refuse the average**. The slide says almost everything else in data feminism follows from that habit.
